The panel previews the next round's newcomers, so the pick is a decision. ④ Pop Beetles (Round 2+): they inflate and beep faster as they near the pile — shoot one far away and it explodes for you, chaining into neighbours (watch for CHAIN ×n); let it arrive and it detonates on the pile for −2. ⑤ Brood Beetles (Round 2+): fat, slow, and they burst into 4 larvae on death — kill them far from the pile, or splash the whole family. ⑥ Room theatre: one crack on your front wall grows through 3 stages as rounds advance, cracks and burrows glow at the rim so beetles pour in from somewhere, and plaster/dirt debris now bounces off your real floor and furniture tops. The 2D prototype below mirrors the same pass (Pop, Brood, mash, Harvest Choice, wall cracks, bouncing debris). The full research — what each idea was stolen from, and what was deliberately not built — is in The fun pass, sourced below.

New in v10.3 — the interaction-model pass (from your v10.2 headset test): ① The menu cannot ambush you anymore, because the triggers that ambushed you no longer exist. Palm-up is deleted outright: seated, your free hand rests in your lap palm-up, fingers open, perfectly still — that IS the “stop” pose, held for seconds, and no threshold can tell resting from intending. The single-hand long-pinch is deleted too (reload-anywhere means constant pinching). In their place: a persistent floating ⏸ MENU button anchored low beside the potato pile, always in the front view — look at it and pinch (or point a hand ray at it and pinch) and the menu opens, with a press animation as feedback. Backup: pinch with BOTH hands together and hold 1 second — gameplay never sustains that — with the fill ring showing progress. The model-independent safeguards stay: triggers only open (never toggle shut), 3 s re-arm after closing, disarmed for a run’s first 2 s and while a Harvest Choice is open, and diagnostics count openings as button / two-hand / game-over / page. ② Menu picks are gaze picks now. You couldn’t select menu items with the arm, so while the menu or a Harvest Choice is open, selection always uses the gaze ray + pinch, in both Aim modes — look at the button (an orange gaze dot and a hover swell show your target) and pinch with either hand. ③ Aim defaults to Head. Three hand-aim variants (grip pose, joint aim, shoulder-line) all lost to head aiming seated — aiming down at floor beetles through a shoulder→hand line puts your hand where your knees are. Head is now the shipped default; the shoulder-line Hand mode still works and stays in the toggle for anyone who wants it — it’s ergonomics, not a bug. Everything else is preserved: wall splats, wall/crack theatre, the fun pass, and the game-over results panel (its buttons are gaze picks too).

New in v10.5 — the fix pass (from your v10.4 headset test): ① Splats can't block shots anymore. The white elongated circle is gone: mash is now an irregular mashed-potato splat (warm pulp colour, darker flecks, a drip smear on walls), and it is a decal + slow-zone ONLY — its raycast is disabled and shots now test beetles along the whole flight path before any surface can stop them, so a beetle behind a splat is always hittable. ② Loading is deterministic, with your requested setting. The phantom auto-reload was a real bug: one physical pinch arrives by two event paths, and the second event was reloading (or upgrading) the gun behind your back — that's also where the random double loads came from. Pinches are now de-duplicated (one pinch = one action), a load in flight ignores further pinches, and nothing loads except: a deliberate pinch in Manual mode (the default — pinch anywhere to load; since v10.21.28 the LEFT hand loads; since v10.21.30 a LEFT fist grab (Meta’s squeeze event) seats a HEAVY), the Auto rule (a new Reload: Manual/Auto toggle in the pause menu and below — Auto loads the next standard round after each shot, never a HEAVY, never mid-gesture, only if the pile can pay), or a power-up effect. And HEAVY is unmistakable now: a deep double-clunk, a floating HEAVY LOADED! callout when it chambers, and a detonation with a double particle burst and shockwave ring. ③ Menu hardened again: the floating MENU button moved far left of the pile and higher — out of your firing sightline — and opens on a pinch-hold (~0.5 s, watch it swell), not an instant pinch; the two-hand trigger now requires both pinches to start within ~150 ms of each other plus the full 1 s overlap, so sequential gameplay pinches can't accumulate into it. If it ever still opens uninvited, the panel now shows a big OPENED VIA: banner at the top — tell me what it says. ④ The white octagon is identified and gone: it was the two-hand gesture fill ring (a white ring + filled disc). It's now a thin amber ring that exists only while a hold is actively accumulating. In its place on your wrist: ⑤ the real wristband radar (your concept, built) — a dark band with a brass-rimmed tracker face on your LEFT wrist: glance down and blips show every beetle in the front field relative to where you're facing (amber standard, red Carrier — pulsing while it carries — gold Golden, flashing Pop), the pile as a potato marker at the bottom, and a slow sweep. The 2D prototype mirrors it as a corner mini-map. ⑥ Room damage is now a system, not a decoration: 3–5 breach sites across your front walls — Round 1 opens only the main breach; each new round activates or grows another, and damage never heals during a run. Every breach is a live spawn front (the main breach spawns most), with the colony behind it: a dark burrow void, warm amber glow, dirt rim, and two glowing eyes ~0.8 s before a beetle pours out. Sealed spawn portals leave permanent scar cracks; debris now lingers ~25 s so wreckage accumulates. Repair is earned: finish a round with zero steals and the Harvest Choice gains a free Patch button; the choice pool also gains a Patch a Breach card that competes with upgrades — a patch seals the newest breach to a scar and removes that front. (And to close your earlier question: the one big permanent crack was always by design — it's the main breach, and it now widens at every round milestone with a plaster burst and a low rumble.)

New in v10.6 — identity & progression (the game becomes its own thing): ① Fiction: no invasion, no sci-fi — the beetle colony nests inside the house walls between the garden and the potato store, and a run is one escalating night defending the harvest store ("Night falls. The colony has found the storehouse."). ② 👑 THE QUEEN — every 3rd round she pours through the main breach: 10 HP, staged shell cracks, stops at 75/50/25% HP to lay egg clusters (shoot the eggs in 5 s or they hatch), and releases a ring of larvae at 25%. ③ Ammo progression, Queen-gated (no shop, no grind): you start with Russet rounds. Fell Queen I → Sweet Potato splash rounds unlock as a selectable ammo; fell Queen II → French Fry rapid mode (self-loading; every shot still costs a potato). Pick ammo at the Harvest Choice after a Queen (and re-pick later); the breech on the gun shows the loaded type — potato, orange sweet, or a fry bundle. The page ammo buttons stay locked until unlocked. ④ Quick-win bundle: a Tank rears up every ~4 s exposing a glowing abdomen for ~1 s — an abdomen hit is an instant kill with a guaranteed power-up orb; a new ❄ Frost orb (12 s of Frost Potatoes: hits freeze a beetle solid 2 s, until a neighbour bumps it free) drops weighted toward precision kills — first-shot and weak-point kills roll bonus orbs; and killing a Carrier within ~1 m of its exit hole triggers a LAST-SECOND SAVE! — brief slow-mo, the potato visibly flying back to the pile, and a clutch-save counter on the game-over panel.

New in v10.4 — the gun art pass (your “cooler and more realistic” ask): the potato gun is rebuilt as a lovingly-built workshop spud cannon. Silhouette: a long brushed-steel barrel up front, a fat steel pressure chamber behind it, a turned-wood rear stock and grip, and a ridged pump grip under the barrel — a real machine, not a toy ray gun. Materials: steel with a procedural scratched/worn finish, polished brass collars, pressure pipe and fittings (the game's established brass, kept), warm wood grain with knots, dark rubber on the pump ridges — and a small procedural reflection environment so the metals actually read as metal in the headset. Details: screws at the joints, a vented muzzle brake, weld rings between sections, a brass maker's plate — and a round pressure gauge on the chamber: its needle rests low when the gun is empty, sits mid when loaded, climbs while a reload seats, jumps on every shot, and sits in the red when a HEAVY round is loaded. Readable state: the loaded potato now sits visibly in an open breech slot on top of the chamber (two stacked for HEAVY) — no UI needed to know you're loaded. Motion: the pump grip slides back and returns as each reload seats (with the usual clunk), and every shot leaves a brief puff of steam at the muzzle alongside the flash and recoil. The 2D prototype's gun is redrawn to match — steel, brass, wood, gauge, breech potato and all. Purely visual: the gun's position, aim, handling and every v10.3 control are untouched.

New in v10.2 — the repair pass (from your v10 headset test): ① The menu can no longer ambush you. It was popping up non-stop during normal play, and the causes were structural: the palm-up trigger needed only ~0.6 s at a loose angle (a grabbing/reaching support hand qualifies), the long-pinch timer also ran off pinches that had just fired or reloaded, and the same gestures could toggle the menu shut again while you pinched its buttons. Now both triggers are deliberate: a long pinch must be one continuous, position-stable hold of a full second (and a pinch that just did gameplay restarts its menu timer from zero); palm-up is a real “stop” gesture — palm square to the ceiling, all fingers open, hand roughly still, held a full second. While either accumulates, a ring at your free hand fills so you can see it coming and drop the gesture to cancel. Gestures only ever open the menu now, they stay disarmed for 3 s after it closes, for the first 2 s of a run, and while a Harvest Choice is open — and the diagnostics now count openings by trigger (“Menu via: long-pinch ×N / palm-up ×M…”), with the last trigger also named on the menu itself, so if anything still misfires it will identify itself. ② Hand aim is a shoulder-line now. v9 made the gun follow your hand, but the barrel took your wrist angle — your own suggestion fixes it: the gun still sits in your hand, but it aims along the line from your shoulder to your hand (shoulder estimated ~22 cm below and ~20 cm to the side of your head, smoothed), so you point with your arm and wrist roll steers nothing. Lightly smoothed against jitter; if joints drop out it falls back to the old joint aim, then gaze. Aim: Head is untouched.

New in v9 — the repair pass (from your v8 test): one root cause sat under two of the three failures. The game reads hand joints from the WebXR frame — but it was fetching that frame through an API this three.js build doesn't have, so the frame silently came back empty on every single frame. Hand poses never loaded, so the Aim toggle had nothing to aim with and the gun always fell back to your gaze; and the joint-distance check that recognises a thumb-to-middle pinch never ran at all (your index pinch only worked because it also arrives as a browser “select” event). The frame now flows in properly, hand poses rebuild every frame, and the HEAVY pinch test is relative — middle fingertip on the thumb, index clearly farther away — instead of demanding your index stay 4 cm clear, which real hands don't do. And game over no longer locks up: the moment the pile empties, your results panel opens in front of you — final score, best combo, Restart run, Exit AR — and the long-pinch / palm-up gestures work after a run ends too, so the panel can always be reopened.

New in v6 — the multi-height, room-aware pass: ① Beetles come out of your real walls and ceiling now. The session requests plane detection, mesh detection, hit-test, anchors, depth sensing and hand tracking as optional features; where your Quest's Space Setup scan gives the game real wall/floor/ceiling planes, cracks split those actual surfaces, beetles crawl on the wall, scuttle down from ceiling corners, then drop to the floor and run for the pile. No scan? A fallback ring keeps the same varied heights on virtual walls, so the game never depends on a scan. ② Hand-joint aiming: the gun is posed from your wrist + index-knuckle joints, so it follows your arm — the diagnostics panel now names the live aim source (hand-joints / grip / target-ray / gaze). ③ Comfort band: no more than about half of spawns are at floor level, and the action is weighted to eye-height wall cracks and mid-distance floor burrows — built for seated play in a chair, a coffee shop, or a plane seat. ④ Pace & juice: beetles roughly a third faster, tighter spawn gaps, mixed-height double spawns in later waves, floating score popups, combo callouts, a warning pulse before a steal — and Carrier beetles: one that reaches the pile grabs a potato and flees with it; shoot it to drop the potato back. ⑤ Art overhaul: the pile is now a real dirt mound (dark soil, clods, pebbles, a burlap rim) instead of a tan disc; floor burrows are cracked dirt mounds, wall spawns are jagged plaster cracks (no more plain round holes); the gun gets oak grain, copper bands, brass fittings and visible recoil.

This is the real version — not the flat prototype below. In AR there is no screen to spin and no pointer: you see your own room through passthrough, the potato pile sits about a metre in front of where you sat down, and beetles emerge across the front 180° only — bursting from jagged cracks in your real walls at seated eye height, scuttling down from ceiling corners, and pushing up out of cracked dirt burrows in the floor — then converge on the pile. The wooden potato gun aims where you look by default (Aim: Head) — or, with the Aim toggle set to Hand, sits in your aiming hand and follows the shoulder-to-hand line. Your other hand does the loading — and it can pinch anywhere: no reaching to the pile, no looking down; a potato arcs from the pile into the gun (listen for the click as it seats). Then pinch with the gun hand to fire.

What to expect from v6, honestly: an earlier note on this page said web pages can't access the Quest's room scan — that was outdated and is corrected here: as of 2026 the Quest Browser supports hit-test, anchors, plane detection with semantic labels, mesh detection, depth sensing and hand-tracking joints, and v6 requests all of them as optional session features (a missing one never blocks the session). If your headset has a Space Setup room scan, expect cracks on your real walls and burrows on your real floor; the diagnostics panel below shows what was actually granted, how many planes/meshes were detected, and whether you're in "real planes" or "fallback ring" mode. Honest limits, updated for v8: floor beetles are furniture-aware now (detected tabletops/desks are climbed over or steered around), but a beetle's path down a wall is still a straight scuttle — it doesn't route around an object mounted mid-wall — and plane quality depends entirely on your room scan. The feel numbers still tune from your headset tests before Nov 18.

Your AR test pass — step by step

  • In the Quest Browser, tap the big button — in the card view it opens the game in a NEW TAB: your diagnostics proved two things — the game was still embedded when AR refused (the view rejected even the request that asked for no features, so the session setup was never the problem), and the v3 escape was BLOCKED because this card page refuses to be replaced. A new tab can't be refused that way. Tap the big button, switch to the new tab it opens (this card copy stays open behind it — ignore it), let the automatic re-check finish there, check the diagnostics “Page view” line says full-page, then tap Enter AR.
  • Sit down first, in the chair you'll play in, with clear space in front of you, and hand tracking turned on in the Quest's quick settings (no controllers in hand). Then tap Enter AR — the pile is placed from where you're sitting when the session starts.
  • If it still won't start: do this check in the new tab, not here — this card copy will always say CARD / embedded, even after a successful escape, because the escape opens a separate tab rather than changing this one. In the new tab, open the diagnostics panel and read “Page view” first: it should say “full-page”. Only then do the session answers mean anything; the game tries six setups, down to a bare request with no options at all, before giving up — and the panel keeps the headset's exact words for me. If no new tab appeared at all, the browser blocked the pop-up: tap the red banner's white button directly (a direct tap on the link itself), and allow pop-ups for this page if the Quest Browser asks.
  • Look left, right, up and down: beetles should appear across the front 180° at mixed heights — jagged cracks splitting your real walls around eye height, corner cracks up high they scuttle down from, and cracked dirt mounds on the floor — roughly half or fewer at floor level, so you're not staring at the ground. Nothing behind you, ever. Wall beetles should stay on the wall, then drop to the floor and run for the pile.
  • Point at a beetle and pinch to fire — you should hear the thump, and a splat when you connect. When the chamber's empty, pinch with your LEFT hand ANYWHERE (new in v8 — no looking down at the pile; the loading hand is the left hand since v10.21.28): a potato arcs from the pile into the gun and the click-clunk means it's loaded.
  • v8 checks: (a) Watch a floor beetle reach your desk — it should climb up the edge, cross the top, and climb down, or steer around the footprint, never crawl through it. The diagnostics now count Furniture planes. (b) HEAVY load: pinch thumb-to-middle-finger — two potatoes stack in the hopper, and the next shot should one-shot a Tank with a big splash (a quick double-pinch with the gun hand works too). (c) Aim toggle: open the pause menu and switch Aim: Hand / Head — Head aims where you look; tell me which you prefer. (d) Power-ups: Golden and Carrier kills sometimes drop a glowing orb — shoot it: gold = French Fry Frenzy (8 s, no reload), orange = Sweet Splash (5 splash shots); the HUD shows what's active.
  • v10 checks: (a) Juice: kills should squash flat with a flash and flying shell chunks; splats should rise in pitch as a combo builds, and a Tank should rock back and show a bigger shell crack with each hit. (b) Mash: fire a shot into the bare floor — a pale splat should stay ~6 s and beetles crossing it should visibly slow. (b2) Wall mash (new in v10.1): now fire a shot into a bare stretch of wall (or, with no room scan, toward the front wall line where wall beetles crawl in) — a pale splat should stick flush on the wall, stretched a little downward like it's sagging, stay ~6 s, and a beetle crawling down that wall through it should visibly slow to half speed. It shares the same pool of 8 splats as the floor ones. (c) Harvest Choice: clear Round 1 — the game should freeze on 3 big cards with an orange “Incoming” preview line; pinch one and Round 2 starts with the resupply. (d) Pop: in Round 2, listen for a beetle whose beeps rise as it inflates — shoot it mid-room and it should explode and chain into neighbours; let one reach the pile and it costs 2. (e) Brood: a fat purple beetle should burst into 4 tiny larvae when killed. (f) Theatre: the big crack on your front wall should be visibly larger in Round 2 than Round 1, and spawn debris should bounce once off the floor/desk instead of falling through.
  • v10.3 checks — the interaction rebuild from your last test: (a) Menu discipline: play a normal, busy stretch — grabbing, reloading, firing, resting your free hand in your lap — and the menu should never appear on its own (the palm-up and long-pinch triggers are deleted, not retuned). Then open it deliberately: look at the orange ⏸ MENU button floating low beside the pile and pinch — it should squash briefly and the menu should open. Close it, and within ~3 s the button should stay dead. Also try the backup: pinch with both hands together and hold 1 second (a ring between your hands fills). (b) Gaze menu picks: with the menu open, LOOK at Resume — the orange dot is your gaze and the button should swell — then pinch with either hand. It must work the same in Aim: Head and Aim: Hand, and for the Harvest Choice cards after a round. (c) Aim default: a fresh run should start in Aim: Head (diagnostics: “mode Head”); floor beetles should be shootable without dropping your hand to your knees. Shoulder-line Hand remains in the 🎯 toggle if you want to compare.
  • v10.5 checks — your v10.4 bug list, one by one: (a) Splat blocking: miss a shot into a wall so a splat sticks, then shoot a beetle crawling behind that splat — the shot must hit the beetle, never the splat; the splat itself should look like irregular mashed potato (creamy tan, flecks, a downward smear), not a white circle. (b) Reload discipline (Manual, the default): fire once and wait — the gun must stay EMPTY until you pinch; a pinch loads exactly one potato; pinch again with your LEFT hand, thumb to middle finger (the one HEAVY gesture since v10.21.28 — a second index pinch no longer stacks) and you should hear the deep clunk, see HEAVY LOADED!, the gauge in the red and two breech potatoes — then the HEAVY shot should detonate visibly bigger (double burst + shockwave ring) and one-shot a Tank. Flip Reload to Auto (page button or pause menu) and the gun should self-load a standard round after each shot — never a HEAVY. (c) Menu (superseded by v10.7): the floating MENU button described here is deleted in v10.7 — opening is the two-hand pinch-hold only; see the v10.7 checks below. (d) Wristband radar: glance at your left wrist — a dark band with a brass-rimmed green radar face: blips should sit on the side the beetles are actually on relative to where you face; Carriers show red, Pops flash. No white octagon should exist anywhere now. (e) Damage: Round 1 = one main breach; Round 2+ = more breaches / growth, spawn eyes glowing ~a second before a beetle pours out of a breach, scars left where portals sealed, debris still lying around late in a wave. Finish a round with zero steals and the Harvest screen should offer a green FREE PATCH button; the Patch a Breach card may also appear among the upgrades.

What's in v8 — this pass, item by item

Furniture awareness (new in v8): detected horizontal planes more than 0.35 m above the floor plane (desks, tabletops, counters) are registered as furniture with a polygon footprint from the plane's own outline. A floor beetle whose path crosses one either climbs it — inched-in edge climb, surface-height crawl across the top, climb down the far side, the same surface-following pattern as wall→floor — or steers around the footprint edge; it no longer crawls through the object's body at floor level. Mesh detection is counted in diagnostics but planes drive the behaviour (noted there too). Fallback ring play (no scan) is unchanged.

Reload anywhere (v8): the LEFT-hand pinch loads from anywhere — the “look down and hover over the pile” step is gone. The fiction and the economy are untouched: a potato still arcs visibly from the pile to the hopper, the load click-clunk still plays, and the pile still pays the cost. The right (gun) hand never loads — it only fires — so a flaky firing-hand read can never seat a round by accident.

Aim: Hand / Head (v8): a toggle in the in-AR pause menu and on the page. Hand = hand-joint aiming; Head = the gun aims along the camera/gaze ray — the feel earlier builds effectively had, which lined up easier. Default is HEAD since v10.3 (three seated hand-aim variants all proved worse ergonomically — floor targets need your hand where your knees are); Hand (shoulder-line) remains available in the toggle, your choice sticks for the session, and diagnostics shows the mode.

HEAVY double-load (v8, Robert's idea): since v10.21.28 the hands are split — the RIGHT hand only fires, the LEFT hand only loads — and the HEAVY has exactly one gesture: a LEFT thumb-to-middle-finger pinch (read from XRHand joint distances — thumb-tip to middle-tip close while thumb-to-index stays open) loads two potatoes for 2 from the pile. The next shot is a heavy splat round: damage 3 (one-shots a Tank), a bigger projectile and a splash radius for neighbours. The hopper shows two stacked potatoes and the HUD chamber reads “HEAVY ×2”. There is no other way to load one: no double-pinch upgrade, no pile hold, no two-hand claim — those paths were retired after the v10.21.27 session's film review showed seats nobody gestured for.

Power-ups (v8): Golden and Carrier kills drop a floating orb about 60% of the time (mid-height, bobbing, ~10 s). Shoot it: French Fry Frenzy — 8 s of rapid fire with no reload, still 1 potato per shot from the pile; or Sweet Splash — the next 5 shots splash. A HUD chip, a gun glow and a distinct activation jingle track what's active.

Test ZIP (v8): the launcher panel's orange button now assembles critter-potato-gun-test.zip in the browser at click time — current page HTML as index.html, the launcher script, and server.js — so it can never ship a stale build; if the ZIP can't be built in a given view it falls back to the standalone game file.

Pause, menu & exit: there was no way to pause or leave a run except quitting through the Quest home menu — that gap is closed. Pinching the floating MENU button beside the pile (gaze or hand ray + pinch), or a two-fist hold, freezes the game and opens a floating panel ~1.2 m in front of you, inside the comfort zone: current score and wave, plus Resume, Restart run, Sound on/off, Aim and Exit AR (session.end()) — all chosen by gaze + pinch. The flat preview gets the same menu via the floating button, the ⏸ Pause / Menu button and mouse clicks. Rebuilt in v10.3: the v7–v10.2 ambient gestures (palm-up, single-hand long-pinch) false-fired across two headset builds — a resting lap hand is indistinguishable from the palm-up pose — so they are deleted, not retuned; the button/two-hand model keeps the 3 s re-arm and via-counting diagnostics.

Audio reliability (fixed): the synthesized engine existed but could sit silent — the AudioContext was never reliably resumed inside the AR flow, and the music timer would run against a suspended clock. Now the context is created/resumed inside the Enter AR tap itself, resumed again on session start and on the first pinch, the music loop only starts once the context is confirmed running, a two-note chirp plays the moment a session starts as an instant sound check, and the diagnostics panel carries a live Audio state line.

Room-aware emergence: every session request now asks (optionally, never required) for hit-test, anchors, plane-detection, mesh-detection, hand-tracking, depth-sensing. Each frame the game reads detectedPlanes / detectedMeshes: vertical planes in the front 180° get jagged wall cracks at 0.4–2.0 m (pinned with an anchor where granted), ceiling planes and wall tops get corner cracks beetles scuttle down from, and floor planes get cracked dirt-mound burrows. With no planes detected, a virtual fallback ring (2.5–3.5 m) supplies the same mix of heights — gameplay never depends on a scan.

Aim: originally posed from XRHand joints (wrist → index knuckle) with a natural held offset at the palm; fallback chain hand-joints → grip space → target-ray → gaze, with the live source shown in diagnostics. Superseded in v10.2 for Hand mode: the barrel now follows the shoulder-to-hand line (see the v10.2 note at the top) — the joint orientation remains only as the fallback when a pointing line can't be formed. Pace: speeds up ~⅓, spawn gaps tightened, waves 2–3 can double-spawn at mixed heights, Wave 1 stays a gentle teacher. New behaviour: Carrier beetles flee with a stolen potato — shoot one to recover it. Score popups, combo callouts and a pre-steal warning pulse on the pile are in. Art: dirt-mound pile with soil texture, clods and a burlap rim; displaced-geometry burrows; jagged plaster wall cracks with dust; oak-and-brass gun with recoil; glossier shells, per-type silhouettes, animated legs and antennae. Still honest limits: wall crawlers take a straight line down to the floor — they don't yet route around a real bookshelf mid-wall — and if the Quest has no room scan the walls are virtual (same heights, same pacing). Pinch forgiveness is unchanged.

What's in v10 — the fun pass, item by item

Juice stack: every kill now squashes the beetle flat (scale Y to ~0.2 in ~80 ms) under a one-frame white flash, with shell-chunk particles on top of the existing splat burst. Splat pitch climbs about a semitone per combo step to ×5 with ±10% randomisation, and when a combo of 5+ ends you hear a “combo banked” chime and see the popup. HEAVY-shot kills (and Pop detonations) trigger ~50 ms of hit-stop — the beetles' clock dips, yours doesn't. Tanks stagger ~0.25 s per hit and grow a visible shell-crack decal per HP lost. Floating callouts: “LONG SHOT!”, “CHAIN ×n!”, “HEAVY!”, same-type streak bonuses. Hard rule honoured: no camera or world shake in MR — the gun recoils and the potato pile wobbles on steals and nearby explosions; the room never moves.

Mash splats — now including walls (v10.1): a shot that hits nothing leaves a pulp decal on the first surface its trajectory actually reaches — the floor or a wall. Missed-shot termination tests each step of the shot's flight against the detected vertical wall planes in the front 180° (the same plane data that carries wall cracks and breaches), plus the floor test, and the nearest impact along the trajectory wins — no more shots flying through walls. Since v10.20.2 detected furniture tops no longer terminate a shot at all: the filled furniture rectangle was eating shots fired down at beetles beside the furniture, so furniture is out of shot resolution entirely — beetles, then walls, then the floor. A wall splat sits flush on that wall, oriented to the plane's normal, stretched with a subtle downward smear so it reads as pulp sagging under gravity (a static smear — no drip simulation). In fallback-ring mode the virtual walls count as wall surfaces too. Life ~6 s (10 s with the Sticky Mash card), one shared cap of 8 across all surfaces, oldest fades first. The slow is surface-agnostic: it is tested by true 3D distance to the splat centre, so a beetle crawling down that wall through a wall splat moves at half speed, exactly like a floor beetle crossing a floor splat. Deliberately weak, so firing at a surface on purpose is never the right play. The 2D prototype mirrors it: a miss on the wall band leaves a smeared wall splat that slows wall-crawlers crossing it.

Harvest Choice: clearing a round freezes the action (same frozen state as pause) and floats 3 cards at ~1.5 m, eye level (v10.12 placement) — pinch one, it lasts the whole run: Stockpile (+3 starting potatoes next round), Bigger Splash (+30% splash radius), Light Heavy (HEAVY costs 1 next round), Lucky Charm (drop chance +50%), Longer Frenzy (+4 s), Sticky Mash (splats last 10 s), Steady Hands (combo window +1 s), Golden Touch (golden beetles worth double). The header previews the next round's incoming types, Plants-vs.-Zombies style. The 2D prototype runs the identical choice as clickable cards.

Pop Beetle: pink, swelling as it closes, beep pitch and rate rising with proximity. Death = explosion damaging everything within ~0.55 m — including other Pops, which chain (depth-capped), with chained kills counting into a distinct CHAIN ×n popup. Reaching the pile alive = self-detonation, −1 potato (blasted visibly off the pile), combo broken, pile wobble.

Brood Beetle: purple, fat, 2 HP, slow. On death it bursts into 4 larvae (tiny fast crawlers, 5 pts) scattering toward the pile — splash and HEAVY blasts clear larvae caught in the same burst, so where you kill it is the decision.

Room theatre: a persistent crack on the front wall (real vertical plane when the scan offers one, fallback position otherwise) swaps through 3 pre-made crack stages and creeps up in scale each round, bursting plaster when it grows. Every spawn crack/burrow gets a glowing rim and a soft outside-glow. All particle debris now bounces once off the real floor height — or a detected furniture top — before settling. The 2D prototype mirrors crack growth on its drawn walls and bounces debris off its floor line.

Also decided: power-up orbs are capped at 3 on the field (Space Pirate Trainer's rule), and shooting an orb to activate it is free — a chamber shot that hits an orb refunds the chamber, so nobody hoards orbs to save ammo.

One file · lives in the Game folder

The Quest test launcher — Start-AR-Test.ps1

The ZIP you asked for: the orange button above builds critter-potato-gun-usb-test-v10.21.37.zip in your browser at click time (the filename carries the version, so kits in your folder read as a timeline) — it fetches this page's own current HTML as the game's index.html, adds the launcher script below and a server.js on port 8901, so the ZIP always contains the newest build, never a stale copy. This ZIP is v10.21.14 — the full .14 fix slate (see the build notes at the top of this page) stacked on v10.21.13's full-slate repair on the v10.21.10 results-panel + input repair (the Keeper's Ledger gets a guaranteed readable layout with no element overlapping another; the deep input audit adds select-channel arbitration, a corroborated rescue and a pile-defence evidence bar; the pile anchor re-bases at the start panel from your settled seated position; white square speckles become soft dirt-toned puffs; the recovery banner names the error it caught) on v10.21.9's moth-lifecycle + pale-material + hold-arming repair (the moth now flies its whole life: a visible swoop dive to the pile and an airborne escape home, never the ground-carrier path; the pale blow-out materials across the roster are re-toned to their authored palettes — the Spitter's sac is deep glossy green with an amber core and its blob a coloured spit wad; the hold-arming widening of that pass (that HEAVY path was retired in v10.21.28)) on v10.21.8's Harvest Choice panel repair (the end-of-round panel now anchors to your seated session centre — yaw AND pitch — instead of wherever your head points when the round ends, and the Harvest Choice and results panels gain the 🧭 Recenter arm-and-lock button) on v10.21.7's repair + input-ergonomics pass from the v10.21.6 session (the pile anchor moves ~0.3 m farther out along your facing — one constant, PILE_FWD217, read by every pile-pinned system — so defending the pile no longer pitches your hands out of the tracking frustum; a hold-to-HEAVY path of that era (retired in v10.21.28 — HEAVY is the left thumb-to-middle pinch only), the middle pinch unchanged; and the reacquire-window debounce: joint dropouts under ~120 ms are bridged instead of restarting the 0.35 s suppression window — the audit confirmed the window WAS restarting on flicker, which is what ate pinches at the frustum edge — with every phantom protection unchanged) on v10.21.6's repair + small UX pass from the v10.21.5 session (the tutorial is now remembered: finished or skipped once, it is never forced again — ▶ PLAY goes straight in, and a 📖 Tutorial button on the start panel replays it on demand; a first-ever browser still gets it, which is the judges' case; a palm-pinch posture hint on the start panel and in the tutorial, because pinching while looking at your open palm opens the Quest's own universal menu; focus-loss recovery hardening with a lost/recovered counter on the Auto-pause diagnostics line, so an OS menu theft un-wedges deterministically; and the full airborne-path audit — a drop-armed beetle is re-seated in its breach's mouth plane, so emergence → drop → first floor step stay on the breach's own vertical line) on v10.21.5's repair pass from the v10.21.4 session footage (Queen arrival staging made unmissable, the glow ring, the absolute true-wall host rule for breaches and scars, the Husk shell, serialized narration, arm-and-lock Recenter, the bigger Ledger, and the deliberate-pinch rescue) on v10.21.4's one-click Copy diagnostics button (on the diagnostics panel in the top game shell) on the v10.21.3 flat-page layout reorder (downloads panel first at the top of the page, Enter AR + diagnostics directly beneath it) on the v10.21.2 freeze-eve repair (drop descent replacing the wall scurry, true-wall breach hosts, the dark colony void and matte scar/plaster family, tracking-loss hardening, the universal text hold, and panel backdrops that contain their content) plus the breach-host distance cap (new breaches host only within 8 m ≈ 26 ft of the session origin; out-of-range rooms fall back to ring hosting), on v10.21's Queen drama, v10.20.2's ring-travel restoration, v10.20's Spud Frenzy, v10.19's comedy pass, v10.18's gun augments and v10.17's character art; it replaces the v10.21 kit. Extract all three files into the Game folder (overwriting), then run the launcher as usual. If the ZIP can't be built in this view, the button falls back to downloading the standalone game file — rename it to index.html in the Game folder.

Yes — the whole routine from your first test (server, port check, adb, Quest serial, reverse tunnel) is now one script. Save it as Start-AR-Test.ps1 in E:\Dev\Muse Development\Critter Potato Gun\Game, right next to index.html — either with the Download button (then move it from Downloads into the Game folder) or by copying the text into a new file of that name. From then on, every test is:

  1. Open one PowerShell window from the Game folder (PowerShell 5 is fine), plug in the Quest.
  2. Run .\Start-AR-Test.ps1 — it finds the Quest itself (no serial to paste), sets the 8901 tunnel, and starts the server in that same window.
  3. In the Quest Browser open http://localhost:8901 and tap Enter AR. Ctrl+C or closing the window stops the server when you're done.

New ZIP while the server is still running? No restart needed. The little Node server re-reads the files from disk on every request — nothing is cached in the server window. So you can extract a new ZIP right over the old files in the Game folder while the server window, the launcher window and the Quest Browser page all stay open. To pick up the new build: exit AR first if you're in it, then reload the page in the Quest Browser — it fetches the fresh index.html from the still-running server. The one exception: if a ZIP ever changed server.js itself, that one file is only read when the server starts — Ctrl+C in the server window and run the launcher again. The game changes in these ZIPs all live in index.html, so reload is all you need.

Same house rules as before, baked in: it uses Android Studio's own adb and never restarts the adb server or kills any process, the tunnel is scoped to your Quest's serial only, the port is our uncommon 8901, and it writes exactly one file — server.js, only if it's missing — inside the Game folder. Nothing touches your Android projects or Codex. If PowerShell refuses with “scripts are disabled on this system”, run it once this way instead: powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\Start-AR-Test.ps1

# Start-AR-Test.ps1 - Critter Potato Gun - Quest AR test launcher # Save this file as Start-AR-Test.ps1 in the Game folder, next to index.html. # Run it from that folder: .\Start-AR-Test.ps1 # One window does everything: checks the files, creates server.js if missing, # waits for the Quest, sets the USB tunnel for port 8901, then runs the # server in this same window. Ctrl+C (or closing the window) stops it. # It uses Android Studio's own adb, never restarts the adb server, never # kills a process, and writes nothing outside this folder - so it stays out # of the way of your other Android projects and anything Codex is running. $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop' $root = $PSScriptRoot if (-not $root) { $root = (Get-Location).Path } Set-Location -LiteralPath $root $port = 8901 Write-Host '' Write-Host '=== Critter Potato Gun - Quest AR test launcher ===' -ForegroundColor Yellow Write-Host "Game folder: $root" if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath (Join-Path $root 'index.html'))) { Write-Host 'index.html is NOT in this folder.' -ForegroundColor Red Write-Host 'Put Start-AR-Test.ps1 in the Game folder, next to index.html, and run it again.' Read-Host 'Press Enter to close' exit 1 } if (-not (Get-Command node -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue)) { Write-Host 'Node.js was not found on PATH. Open a window where node works, then run the script again.' -ForegroundColor Red Read-Host 'Press Enter to close' exit 1 } $serverPath = Join-Path $root 'server.js' if (-not (Test-Path -LiteralPath $serverPath)) { $serverJs = @' const http = require('http'), fs = require('fs'), path = require('path'); const root = __dirname; const types = { '.html': 'text/html', '.js': 'text/javascript', '.css': 'text/css', '.png': 'image/png', '.jpg': 'image/jpeg', '.webp': 'image/webp' }; http.createServer((req, res) => { let p = decodeURIComponent(req.url.split('?')[0]); if (p === '/') p = '/index.html'; const f = path.join(root, p); if (!f.startsWith(root)) { res.writeHead(403); return res.end('forbidden'); } fs.readFile(f, (e, d) => { if (e) { res.writeHead(404); return res.end('not found'); } res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': types[path.extname(f)] || 'application/octet-stream' }); res.end(d); }); }).listen(8901, '127.0.0.1', () => console.log('Serving ' + root + ' at http://localhost:8901')); '@ Set-Content -LiteralPath $serverPath -Value $serverJs -Encoding utf8 Write-Host 'Created server.js (serves this folder on port 8901).' -ForegroundColor Green } $already = Get-NetTCPConnection -LocalPort $port -State Listen -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue if ($already) { Write-Host "Port $port is already listening - a server may already be running. The tunnel will still be set up below; a second server will not be started." -ForegroundColor Yellow } $adb = $null $adbCandidate = Join-Path $env:LOCALAPPDATA 'Android\Sdk\platform-tools\adb.exe' if (Test-Path -LiteralPath $adbCandidate) { $adb = $adbCandidate } else { $adbCmd = Get-Command adb -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue if ($adbCmd) { $adb = $adbCmd.Source } } if (-not $adb) { Write-Host 'adb.exe was not found (looked in the Android Studio SDK location and on PATH).' -ForegroundColor Red Read-Host 'Press Enter to close' exit 1 } Write-Host "adb: $adb" Write-Host '' Write-Host 'Plug the Quest into the PC with USB-C, put the headset on, and tap Allow on the USB debugging prompt.' -ForegroundColor Cyan $serial = $null for ($i = 0; $i -lt 30 -and -not $serial; $i++) { $questLine = (& $adb devices -l) | Select-String 'model:Quest_3' | Select-Object -First 1 if ($questLine) { $serial = ($questLine.ToString() -split '\s+')[0] } if (-not $serial) { Write-Host 'Waiting for the Quest...'; Start-Sleep -Seconds 2 } } if (-not $serial) { Write-Host 'The Quest was not seen after about a minute. Check the cable, that the headset is awake and unlocked, and that you tapped Allow - then run the script again.' -ForegroundColor Red Read-Host 'Press Enter to close' exit 1 } Write-Host "Quest found: $serial" -ForegroundColor Green & $adb -s $serial reverse tcp:8901 tcp:8901 Write-Host 'USB tunnel (Quest localhost:8901 to this PC):' -ForegroundColor Green & $adb -s $serial reverse --list Write-Host '' if ($already) { Write-Host 'A server is already listening on 8901, so there is nothing else to start.' Write-Host 'In the Quest Browser, open: http://localhost:8901 then tap Enter AR.' -ForegroundColor Cyan Read-Host 'Press Enter to close' exit 0 } Write-Host 'Starting the server in this window - leave it open while you play.' -ForegroundColor Green Write-Host 'In the Quest Browser, open: http://localhost:8901 then tap Enter AR.' -ForegroundColor Cyan Write-Host 'Stop everything with Ctrl+C or by closing this window.' Write-Host '' & node (Join-Path $root 'server.js')
Audit v10.8 · Stability pass — no new features

Everything checked, what was fixed, what was verified clean

Robert asked for a full pass over the whole game — AR build and 2D mirror — to make the code solid. This section is the record: the areas audited, the bugs found and fixed (with their class), what was verified clean, the feature inventory against the research roadmap, and the honest known-limits. The v10.7 fix pass (freeze / menu / radar / chair) landed immediately before this audit and is listed first.

v10.7 — the fix pass (from the v10.6 headset test)

  • Freeze — per-run accumulation (resource leak class). Restarts used scene.remove() only: geometry, materials and — biggest of all — one fresh canvas texture per score popup stayed allocated forever. Fixed: a single disposal path (killMesh/disposeObj) now removes and disposes every per-run object; textures are disposed only when created for that one object (popups, story banners, Tank decals), never when shared (beetle skins, mash pulp, cached crack stages). Every spawnable list is hard-capped, oldest-first: beetles 42, particles 140, debris 40, splats 8, eggs 24, popups 14, ghosts 10, shots 24, orbs 3 (pre-existing), scars 26 (pre-existing).
  • Freeze — silent failure (missing fault barrier). The frame loop now runs inside a watchdog try/catch: an exception is logged to diagnostics with its message, the game phase and live object counts; a “Recovered from a hiccup” banner shows in-headset; the game recovers to the pause menu; a 1.5 s render-only hold breaks error loops. Live object counts are in diagnostics, refreshed every second — a slow leak is now visible in a screenshot.
  • Freeze lookalike — tracking loss. Both hands untracked for >3 s mid-run now auto-pauses behind a big HANDS LOST panel and resumes after ~0.3 s of steady tracking, instead of leaving a dead-looking world.
  • Menu — competing pointers (input-model class). The floating MENU button is deleted outright: two-fist hold (1 s) is the only in-AR opener, plus the automatic game-over panel and the page Pause button for flat play. Single-cursor rule: menu/choice/results open ⇒ gun holstered + aim ray hidden ⇒ the gaze dot is the only pointer, and hover highlight and pinch selection read that same ray. Button/card hitboxes enlarged beyond their drawn art.
  • Radar — geometry intersection. The band was a fat tilted torus whose front arc passed through the face. Rebuilt as a watch: face proud at z +0.0165 on a case (z 0.004–0.016); band torus in the strap plane centred z −0.045: centreline arc reaches z +0.003, tube surface z +0.014 — behind the case front (+0.016) and the face (+0.0165), never over the face. Verified by construction (z-order assertion in the regression checks).
  • Chair beetles — hit volume inside its surface (spatial-consistency class). Wall/ceiling/furniture-face beetles rendered half-sunk in their crawl plane with the hit centre inside it. They now spawn pushed proud of the surface along its normal by ~body radius (rendered position = hit-test position), and the projectile’s surface allowance is the beetle’s own body radius instead of a flat 4% of the step.

v10.8 — audit findings: fixed

  • Lifecycle: XR session-end left transient state behind (mid-Choice panel, hands-lost flag, held-select and joint pinch state, a pending auto-load timer). All are now torn down in the session end handler; re-entering AR twice in a row starts clean. Enter AR is guarded against double-start while a session is live.
  • Lifecycle: hiding the page mid-run (tab switch / headset sleep) left the run playing unseen. A visibilitychange handler now auto-pauses a live run.
  • Input integrity: selectend cleared the select state but not the joint edge-detect state for that hand — a stale pinch could survive a session boundary. Both now reset together. (The original double-event class — one pinch via select + joint paths — was already gated in v10.5; the audit re-verified every handler: pinch, middle pinch, two-hand hold and gaze selection are each idempotent per physical gesture.)
  • Numeric safety: a beetle whose position goes NaN/Infinity (bad joint or plane frame) is now removed at the top of its update instead of propagating; fire() rejects non-finite directions; the radar skips non-finite blips; accuracy was already divide-by-zero guarded; frame delta was already clamped to 50 ms.
  • Performance: the aim ray rebuilt its geometry attribute (a new GPU buffer) every frame via setFromPoints; it now updates the existing attribute in place.
  • 2D mirror: the flat prototype’s particle/popup lists were uncapped; they now trim to 420 / 24 in its step loop. Its countdown and rehearsal timers are one-time page singletons.

Verified clean (checked, no change needed)

  • Listeners & timers: every addEventListener is either a one-time page/session registration or attached to a per-session object that dies with the session; the music interval is a singleton cleared by musicStop; the 1 s diagnostics interval is a page singleton; no per-run interval exists.
  • Phase machine: idle → playing → paused / choice → playing → over → restart / exit all reach a known state; game over auto-opens the results panel (the v8 lock-up cannot recur — the panel accepts phase over and the two-fist hold reopens it).
  • Fallbacks: no room scan ⇒ fallback-ring spawns at the same mixed heights; planes not granted ⇒ same path; mesh detection is counted for diagnostics only and nothing depends on it; hand-tracking absent ⇒ input arrives as none-handed selects and the gun rides the gaze (Head aim is the default) — playable end to end. Diagnostics report granted features, plane/mesh counts and room mode truthfully.
  • Regression (headless): all inline scripts parse; the disposal/cap/watchdog/holster code paths assert present; swept-segment and wall-impact math re-checked; shoulder-line aim still wrist-invariant; menu gates (two-fist simultaneity + 1 s + re-arm) unchanged; radar z-order asserted. Restart soak is verified by construction: a restart disposes every per-run list and every list is capped, so object counts return to baseline — the on-headset 10-restart soak is on Robert’s test list (checklist above) to confirm in the real renderer.

Performance & hosting notes (Quest 3)

  • Draw calls are bounded by the hard caps above; the radar canvas redraws at most ~4×/s (256²); menu/choice textures redraw only when a panel opens or a toggle flips; popup textures are capped at 14 alive and disposed on expiry.
  • The exported game is a single self-contained HTML file. Its only runtime network dependencies are the ones it already had: the three.js and JSZip CDNs and Google Fonts. A judges’ host must allow those CDNs — nothing else is fetched at runtime. Flagged honestly: the test ZIP contains index.html + launcher + server.js only, so the hub page’s hero image (assets/hero.webp) is not in the ZIP — in the test folder that one hub image may not load; the AR game itself is unaffected.

Known limits (honest)

  • The chair case: beetles can only crawl on surfaces the room scan reports. A chair back/leg that is scanned as a vertical plane is now hittable (v10.7 proud-offset fix). A chair that is not in the Space Setup scan has no surface in code at all — a beetle “on” it is on the wall/floor behind it, and the fix cannot invent the chair. Re-scan the room including the chair, or treat it as a scan gap, not a hit bug.
  • No room scan = fallback ring (measured Nov 12, 2026): Robert’s test session was granted plane-detection and mesh-detection but detected 0 planes / 0 meshes — the room ran entirely in the virtual fallback ring, which points at a missing or stale Quest Space Setup scan rather than a game bug. The game plays identically in the ring (same heights, pacing and breaches), but real-wall breaches need a current scan: Settings → Environment setup → Space settings (the current Horizon OS route — Robert navigated it in-headset on Nov 12, 2026; older notes on this page that said “Physical Space → Space Setup” predate the current menus). Since v10.10 the game also says this in-headset (one-time Room Check notice ~10 s into a session that still sees no planes).
  • Wall-descent paths are straight scuttles — beetles don’t route around objects mounted mid-wall. Mesh detection is counted, not yet used for routing.
  • The radar orients by billboarding toward the player from the tracked wrist position — readable at a glance, but not a true wrist-axis watch orientation.
  • The restart soak is verified by construction + static assertion headlessly; the definitive 10-restart soak happens on Robert’s headset (checklist item above).

Addendum — v10.9 charm pass (additive only)

The v10.9 pass (Keeper’s Ledger, grade + near-miss, reactive lines, proximity line, micro-personality, pile/wall life, One More Night, radar pace marker) was built strictly additively on this audited build: no stability system, input path or menu rule was modified, refactored or removed — the only removals are the per-run scar sweep (scars became session-scoped, still capped and disposed on eviction) and display text. The rollback point is this v10.8 audit build.

Persistence decision: the research’s proximity item allows one versioned localStorage blob; the audit’s judgement was to scope it down to session-memory bests (best score/grade/round, Queens beaten, runs played) — zero storage risk in any headset context, nothing depends on it, and it covers the sitting-length retry loop the feature exists for. Stated here so the gap is explicit, per the audit’s own rules.

Sourced from (full report: research_notes/replayability-charm-little-things-resear-20261112-0526): Balatro’s end-screen and instant restart; Hades’ reactive dialogue and bosses who remember (Megaera); near-miss psychology (Cambridge Neuron work, via TechOracle); Vampire Survivors / Balatro Collection unlock proximity; Angry Birds’ per-level grades; Mario Kart’s ghost, in stat form only; Game Developer’s idle-animation survey; Untitled Goose Game / Job Simulator reaction comedy; First Encounters’ end screen (Score / Caught / Highest Combo).

The fun pass · Designed from research, not vibes

What the best wave-defense games actually do — and what got stolen

You asked what would make this more than “minimally basic”, so the mechanics of the genre's best were researched properly — First Encounters, Space Pirate Trainer, Blasters of the Universe, In Death, Plants vs. Zombies, Vampire Survivors, Little Critters, Metro 2033 and the game-feel literature. The headline finding: the games that stay fun do not escalate by “more + faster + tougher” — they escalate by composition. Each new enemy invalidates the player's current habit and demands a different decision. Adding enemies is, in one wave-design analysis's words, “the weakest difficulty lever”; changing what enemies demand is the strongest. You approved the ranked top-5 plus the room-theatre item; those are what's in v10, in both builds where they fit.

1 · The juice stack

From Juice It or Lose It (Jonasson & Purho): squash, flash, particles, pitch and hit-stop transform an unchanged ruleset. A 3,018-player dose study found medium/high juice beats both none and extreme. The negative control is Elven Assassin — reviewers savaged its big enemies for absorbing hits “via a health bar… no stagger animation, nothing.” Hence: squash + flash + chunks on every kill, a combo pitch ladder, ~50 ms hit-stop on HEAVY kills, and Tanks that stagger and crack visibly per HP. In MR the shake goes on the gun and the pile — never the passthrough world.

2 · Mash splats — misses buy ground

The economy's worst moment is paying a potato for a clean miss. Little Critters' Toe Jammer goo (a slow-zone other systems feed on) suggested the fix: a missed shot that reaches a surface leaves a mash splat that halves beetle speed for ~6 s. Since v10.1 "a surface" includes walls — the splat sticks flush to the wall plane the shot actually hit, smeared slightly downward, and slows beetles crawling down that wall. Deliberately weak — a consolation, capped at 8, never a strategy.

3 · Harvest Choice — pick 1 of 3

Vampire Survivors' pause-and-pick-1-of-3 and Little Critters' survive-a-wave → level-up reward are the cheapest “one more run” engines in the research. Clearing a round now freezes the action on 3 big pinch cards from a pool of 8 run-only upgrades — plus Plants vs. Zombies' trick of telegraphing the next wave's types, so the pick is a counter-decision, not a guess.

4 · Pop Beetle — the chain engine

In Death's exploding heads and PvZ's Jack-in-the-Box zombie: a kamikaze whose correct play flips with distance. Shot far away, it's a free bomb for you; at the pile, it costs 2 potatoes. Inflation + rising beeps telegraph it, and Pops chain into each other — the CHAIN ×n moments are the screenshots.

5 · Brood Beetle — kill location matters

PvZ's Gargantuar throws an Imp deep into your defence at a damage threshold; tower-defense splitters spawn minis on death. The Brood bursts into 4 larvae wherever it dies — safe at range, a disaster on the pile, and a showcase for splash/HEAVY shots that clear the whole family in one blast.

6 · Room theatre — the room loses

First Encounters' wow is not a weapon system — it's that the room visibly loses: walls crack progressively, things crash through the ceiling, rubble bounces off your real furniture. Faked at plane level here: a persistent front-wall crack growing through 3 stages, glowing rims on every spawn hole, and debris that bounces once off your real floor and furniture tops.

Balance rules copied wholesale

  • Power-ups capped at 3 on the field, tightly timed, never permanent in-run — Space Pirate Trainer's exact discipline (Machine Gun 10 s, Shield 15 s, Gravity Field 20 s, Homing 10 s…). Permanence lives in the Harvest Choice pool instead, and the two pools look different.
  • Orb activation is a free shot — sources describe SPT's activation method inconsistently (shoot the crate vs. touch it); we picked shoot-to-activate and made the chamber refund explicit so using a power-up never costs a potato.
  • Escalation order: composition > compression > count — new demands first (Brood R2, Pop R2), tighter gaps second, raw numbers last. One new threat at a time, with waves of focus before mixing.
  • Your HEAVY double-load is Metro 2033's military-grade round — premium ammo that is literally money. Metro's documented failure mode is the warning: if scarcity is total, the choice disappears — hence resupply, refunds-by-streak (same-type streak of 3 = +1 🥔) and golden gambles keeping an income floor under the economy.

Honestly unverified — and deliberately not built

  • First Encounters' power-ups: no authoritative source describes puffian types, weapon changes or a power-up system for it — credible coverage treats it as a single-weapon timed score attack. It's cited here only for room theatre, colour combos and session shape; any claim it has power-ups would be speculation.
  • Not built, by your call: the shareable end-of-run score card and anything multiplayer (Space Pirate Trainer DX's Arena needs a 10×10 m space and a second player — incompatible with seated solo play anyway).
  • Researched but held for after the deadline: the Leaf-Shield Beetle with its Piercing Spuds counter (a pair, ~2 days), freeze rounds, the Spitter Beetle, the Queen boss (assembly of tank + layer + mite parts), free trap placement (Little Critters' full system is a project of its own), and permanent meta-progression (Elven Assassin's most-criticised system — run-only choices give the variety without the grind).
  • Little Critters' full roster and exact numbers weren't available from an authoritative source, so none are asserted — only its documented traps, slimeball economy and level-up rewards.

Sources, read Nov 11–12, 2026: Meta — First Encounters developer story · Meta Quest Blog — Little Critters · Space Pirate Trainer — Steam Tips & Tricks guide (droid/power-up lists) · UploadVR — SPT high-score tips · LootGames — Plants vs. Zombies counters guide · Playtested — Vampire Survivors genre review · Destructoid — Metro 2033 bullets-as-currency · Game feel & juice dose research summary · Reign Creative — wave-survival design

Playable prototype — the illustrated build

They burst through your walls — a 180° seated invasion

The quality bar is Meta’s First Encounters — the Quest 3 demo where the little aliens crash through your ceiling and walls — and the build now plays that way. The room is the same warm, lamplit living room as the thumbnail, widened into a panorama that wraps left and right walls around you. Beetles burst out of it: cracks split the plaster, holes open in the ceiling and they drop in on silk threads, burrows pop in the floorboards, and the bookshelf, sofa, picture frame and curtains all leak critters — each arrival with a puff of plaster or dirt. This is also your demo-video stage set: the shots in the Day 6 plan below are all framed on this loop.

Simplified: hands only, two pinches, nothing else. The hold-to-pull bolt step is gone, and so are the keyboard keys and the extra Grab button. There are now only two moves, both done by pointing and pinching (in this browser: tapping): pinch a potato in the pile to grab it — it loads itself — then pinch a beetle to fire. That’s the whole gun. The critters have also been rebalanced to match: slower, arriving less often, with a breather at the start of every wave, and Wave 1 is a deliberate training wave. Follow the orange coach bar directly under the game — it always tells you the one thing to do next.

How the gun works now: in the headset, one hand holds and aims the gun while the other hand reaches out, grabs a potato from the pile and drops it in — then a pinch on the trigger fires. On this 2D screen the same two moves are two taps: tap the pile, tap a beetle. No holding, no dragging, no keys, no buttons to load or fire. The full hand mapping is in The potato gun, simplified below.

Three frames are drawn over the room, because the glasses spec is three layers deep. The wide amber frame is the 180° front field: seated and facing one way, the whole invasion plays across the front panorama — left wall to right wall, ceiling to floor — and nothing ever comes from behind you, per the competition’s seated-play rules. The middle frame is the 70° glasses view — everything the Meta VR Glasses can show at once. Inside it, the white dashed frame is the 58° × 54° core: the pile, the gun, the shooting and the splat feedback live in that centre, so you aim and score in one settled gaze while the wide field supplies the First Encounters spectacle around it — beetles converge into the core as they close on the pile. The white ring is the 2-foot seated radius: pile, gun and both hands stay inside it, no standing, stepping, or leaning out of the chair. Every shot still costs potatoes (1–2 by ammo, paid when you grab it from the pile), and every beetle that reaches the pile steals 1 and breaks your combo.

1 PINCH THE PILE — grab

When the gun is empty, point at a potato in the pile (bottom centre, on the rug) and pinch / tap it. That’s the grab — like reaching out and picking one up. Cost: 1 potato (2 for Sweet Potato).

2 IT LOADS ITSELF

Do nothing — the potato you pinched flies into the gun and loads on its own, in about a tenth of a second. When the coach bar says “Loaded”, you’re ready. No second gesture, no button.

3 PINCH A BEETLE — fire

Point at the beetle you want to hit and pinch / tap it. That pinch is the trigger — the gun fires straight at that spot, instantly. Then pinch the pile again for the next potato.

Hands only — no keyboard, no load/fire buttons. Follow the orange coach bar above: gun empty → pinch / tap the potato pile and it loads itself; gun loaded → pinch / tap a beetle and it fires at that spot. Two pinches per shot, that’s all. Critters are slower and spawn further apart in this pass, and every wave opens with a short breather, so that rhythm comfortably keeps up in Wave 1.

Is this the real room version — or a mock-up?

Honest answer: this page is a 2D browser mock-up of the game — a prototype you can play in a window (including inside Muse) to prove the rules, the pacing and the framing before the headset build. It is not yet the mixed-reality experience in your real room. That distinction matters for exactly the thing you noticed: distance and two real hands.

Here, in this mock-up

  • A drawn living room on a flat screen — the pile and gun are close together at the bottom of the picture
  • One pointer / pinch does the work of both hands: tap the pile to grab, tap a beetle to fire — two taps, no holding or dragging
  • Beetles cross a few inches of screen, so everything feels faster and more cramped than it will in a room
  • Its job: test whether the loop is fun, readable and keep-up-able — which is why the pacing was just slowed down here first

In the headset version — v2 is built, above

  • Passthrough: beetles emerge across the front 180° of your real room, metres away — not inches. The AR build at the top of this page is that version's first testable cut
  • That distance is reaction time: a beetle crossing a real room takes far longer to reach the pile than one crossing this screen
  • Both hands tracked at once: the gun rides your aiming hand and points where it points, your other hand pinches at the pile to grab a potato, and a pinch fires
  • Same rules, same costs — learned here, then played for real in the room

So learn the rhythm here where a miss costs nothing, and judge the feel — the reach, the distance, the two hands working together — on the Quest pass. If the cycle still can’t keep up at the new, slower pacing here, it gets simplified (one-pinch fire) rather than shipped frustrating.

The gun · Simplified — hands only

Grab a potato. Pinch to fire. That’s the whole gun.

The earlier version made you hold to pull a bolt back between grabbing and firing — an extra step that was easy to miss and too slow against a wave. It’s gone. One hand holds and aims the gun; the other hand does one thing — reach to the pile and grab a potato. Loading is automatic the moment you grab, and firing is a single pinch on the trigger, aimed wherever you’re pointing. Two moves, both big and readable to hand tracking. Against critters that now take roughly 10 seconds to cross to the pile in Wave 1, two quick pinches per shot is comfortably keep-up-able.

1 · Grip & aim — lead hand

Point the whole gun

Hold the grip and point. The aim ray comes off the barrel, not your finger, so where the gun points is where the potato goes. The gun, pile and crosshair all sit inside the 58° × 54° core — aiming never asks for a head turn. In the browser: move your pointer to aim.

2 · Grab — support hand

Tap the pile, potato loads itself

Reach to the pile (inside the 2 ft radius, low-centre) and close your hand on a spud — it arcs into the hopper on its own. The cost leaves the pile at the grab — 1 potato, 2 for a sweet potato. On this screen: tap a potato in the pile.

3 · Load — automatic

It drops in by itself

No gesture, no button, no hold. The grabbed potato arcs into the hopper and the chamber is loaded in about a tenth of a second. In the headset this is the support hand dropping the spud in; on screen it just happens, so your attention stays on the beetles.

4 · Fire — pinch the trigger

Point at a beetle, pinch

Point the gun at the beetle and pinch — that pinch is the trigger pull, and the shot fires instantly at that spot. Recoil, muzzle flash, chamber empty. Pinch the pile for the next potato. On this screen: tap the beetle. Menus are the same single pinch.

Built to the glasses spec · Competition fit

Seated. Front 180°. Nothing behind you, ever.

The competition asks for a game you can sit down and play, so the design follows the Meta VR Glasses recommendations as hard rules, not guidelines. A full 360° version is the dream for later — this build deliberately is not one.

RuleWhat it means hereHow the build honours it
Seated, stationaryPlayable from one chair, facing one way, no locomotionNo walking, no teleporting, no turning around. Every interaction — aim, grab, pull, menus — happens in front of the chair inside a 2 ft radius.
180° front fieldThe whole world lives in the front hemisphereBeetles burst in across the full front panorama — left wall, right wall, ceiling, floor, furniture. Spawn code has no “behind” to pick from.
70° glasses viewWhat the glasses can show at any one momentDrawn as the middle guide frame. Wide-field spawns are spectacle; anything a beetle does that matters — closing on the pile — plays out as it converges into this view.
58° × 54° coreThe central safe area for essential playPile low-centre, gun and crosshair, combo and score feedback, and the final approach of every beetle all stay inside the core. If losing sight of it would cost you the game, it lives in here.
Hands onlyNo controllers, anywherePinch only: pinch the pile to grab & auto-load, pinch a target to fire, one pinch for menus with big targets. No hold step, no keyboard, no load/fire buttons.
Smooth & comfortableFirst Encounters feel: fluid, physical, aliveBeetles physically emerge — cracks, ceiling drops on silk, floor burrows, debris bursts — with waddle, squash and splat feedback, and no artificial camera motion of any kind.
Day 5 · Field-of-view polish

Three frames: 180° of invasion, 70° of view, 58° × 54° of play

The glasses give you a narrow window inside a wide room, so Day 5 designs in layers instead of pretending the window is the world. The 180° front field is where the invasion happens — beetles can burst in anywhere across the front panorama, because turning your head left, right, up or down while seated is comfortable and fun. The 70° glasses view is what the glasses show at once. And the 58° × 54° core is where the game is actually played: pile, gun, crosshair, combo, score cues and bonus menus all live there, and every beetle's final approach to the pile crosses it. Spectacle may roam the 180°; nothing essential ever leaves the core — and nothing, at any layer, exists behind the player.

Front view — what the seated player actually sees

■ Core 58° × 54° — essential play70° glasses view — everything visible at once180° front field — spawns & spectacle
58° × 54°

Core safe area

All essential play. The pile sits low-centre inside it with the gun, crosshair and both hands; every menu button, score cue and combo warning renders inside it, and every beetle's final approach crosses it. If it matters, it's in here.

70°

The glasses view

Everything the Meta VR Glasses can show at one moment, wrapped around the core. Beetles travelling in from the wide field become visible here in good time — no pop-in at the core's edge, no ambushes from outside the glass.

180°

Front field — seated

The invasion's stage: left wall to right wall, ceiling to floor, all in front of the chair. Beetles burst in anywhere across it — that's the First Encounters spectacle — then converge on the pile. Behind the player: nothing. There is no spawn, sound cue or prompt that ever asks you to turn around.

Day 5 · Seated end-to-end test

One chair. A 2-foot radius. The whole loop.

The test that decides whether the polish worked. Mark a 2 ft radius (4 ft across) on the floor around the chair — tape or a rug edge is fine. Everything in the game, from the first pinch to the restart, has to be playable from inside that circle. Run it in the Quest browser with Seated test turned on in the prototype above; the same steps apply to the headset build.

1

Set the circle, sit down

Chair centred in the taped 2 ft radius. Sit, feet inside the circle. Pile position should land at comfortable arm's reach — no leaning forward to “meet” it.

2

Check the frames before you play

With FOV guides on, confirm the white 58° × 54° core frame is fully visible in one settled gaze — top HUD, both side guides, and the pile at the bottom — then look left, right, up and down to confirm the 180° field is all front, all comfortable, nothing behind.

3

Play Round 1 end to end

Start from the menu, clear all 3 waves, pinch a round-end bonus. Switch ammo at least once — and use only pinches for every shot: pinch the pile to grab, pinch a beetle to fire. Beetles may burst in anywhere across the front field, but every one you actually shoot should be inside the core.

4

Force the failure path

Let the pile drain (or spray it empty) to reach game over, then restart with one pinch — still seated, still inside the circle. The loop isn't end-to-end until restart is.

5

Log it, then tune one thing

Fill in the run log below. If anything failed, change exactly one thing — pull a spawn line in, raise the pile, enlarge a target — and re-run. No batch fixes.

Pass criteria — all five, or it doesn't pass

  • Full round + bonus pick + game over + restart completed without standing, stepping out, or leaning outside the 2 ft radius
  • Every beetle arrives from the front 180° — zero spawns behind or beside the chair, zero “where did that come from?” steals
  • Pile, combo and score readable in the same settled gaze inside the 58° × 54° core, no head turn required
  • Every shot done with two pinches only — pinch the pile, pinch the target — plus all other pinch targets (ammo, menus, restart) reachable and hittable seated, first try most of the time
  • No discomfort, no reaching strain, and no urge to turn around at any point in the run

If it fails

Beetle stole before you saw it? Its path skirted the core — bend convergence paths inward. Pile clipped at the bottom? Raise it inside the core. Reaching? The target is outside the 2 ft ring — move the game, not the player.

RunSetupResultWhat to note
Run 1 — baselineSeated test on · FOV guides on☐ Pass   ☐ FailFirst spawn you missed, if any — and where it appeared
Run 2 — after one tuneSame chair, same circle☐ Pass   ☐ FailThe single change you made, and whether the same failure recurred
Run 3 — guides offFOV guides off · play blind☐ Pass   ☐ FailDoes it still feel contained without the frame drawn? That's the shipping check

Recording checklist

  • Before: headset charged, lenses cleaned, room quiet, notifications off, 2 ft radius taped, FOV guides on for the fit shot only
  • Capture raw, edit down: record each segment long, trim in the edit — never try to perform the exact timing live in the headset
  • Keep game audio under the voice — splats audible, voice clearly on top; check on phone speakers, not just headphones
  • Captions on — judges may watch muted; auto-caption, then fix “pinch”, “russet” and “Critter Potato Gun” by hand
  • Export check: 1080p, total runtime displayed under 3:00 before upload, first frame is gameplay (not a title card)
  • Retake triggers: the grab → load → pinch-to-fire sequence not visible in the setup shot · pile counter off-screen in any ammo beat · a segment where you explain a feature instead of showing it
