Devpost field

Project name

Critter Potato Gun
Devpost field

Elevator pitch / tagline

Potato beetles are stealing your potatoes in mixed reality — defend the pile with a two-hand potato gun that fires the very potatoes they're after. Grab a potato, pinch to fire. Seated, hands only, no controllers.
Devpost field · About the project

Inspiration

I wanted a mixed-reality game you understand in five seconds: critters are in your room, they're stealing your potatoes, shoot them. Mixed-reality critter games have already shown how readable and funny that loop is — so the question I set myself was what a genuinely new mechanic on top of it would look like. The answer became the whole game: the ammo is the thing being stolen. Every potato you fire is a potato the beetles don't have to steal, and every potato they steal is one you can't fire. That single tradeoff turned a wave shooter into a resource game, and it's why the pile — not a health bar — sits at the centre of everything.
Devpost field · About the project

What it does

Critter Potato Gun is a hands-first mixed-reality game for Meta VR Glasses and Meta Quest. Potato beetles burst out of the player's real walls, ceiling, floor and furniture and head for a pile of potatoes. The player defends the pile with a potato gun: one hand holds the grip and aims, the other grabs a potato from the pile and drops it in (loading is automatic), and a pinch on the trigger fires. No controllers anywhere — menus are one-pinch. Each shot costs potatoes from the pile (1–2 depending on ammo, paid when the potato is grabbed and loaded), and each beetle that reaches the pile steals one and breaks the player's combo. There are three ammo types — a standard Russet, a two-potato Sweet Potato with splash damage, and a rapid, light French Fry — plus a HEAVY double-load (thumb-to-middle-finger pinch stacks two potatoes into one splash round that one-shots a Tank), and power-up orbs dropped by Golden and Carrier kills that trigger timed French Fry Frenzy or Sweet Splash rounds when shot. The roster runs to nine behaviours: Crawlers, zig-zagging Dashers, swaying Weavers, crouch-and-spring Hoppers, three-hit armoured Tanks that stagger and crack visibly per hit, potato-carrying Carriers, rare Golden Beetles worth bonus points and bonus potatoes — and, from Round 2, Pop Beetles that inflate, beep and chain-explode, and Brood Beetles that burst into four larvae on death. Missed shots leave mash splats that slow beetles crossing them. Play runs in rounds of three escalating waves; chained hits build a score multiplier up to ×5, clearing a round freezes the action on a Harvest Choice — three big pinch cards from a pool of eight run-long upgrades, with the next round's newcomers previewed — and an empty pile is game over, with results and a one-pinch restart. The whole game is designed seated, for the competition's front-only play: the invasion fills a 180° front field (nothing ever spawns behind the player), the glasses show a 70° view of it at any moment, and all essential play — the pile, the gun, the shooting — sits inside a 58° × 54° core safe area within a 2-foot reach radius.
Devpost field · About the project

How I built it

Built solo with the Immersive Web SDK (WebXR) — no engine install, iterating in the browser. Hand tracking does everything: the lead hand's grip ray aims the gun, and the support hand feeds it — a grab at the pile loads a potato automatically (and pays its cost), and a pinch on the trigger fires at whatever the gun is pointing at. Every menu choice is the same single pinch on one large target; there is no hold step, no keyboard and no button-driven loading or firing. Scene understanding places beetle spawn points on the room's real surfaces — walls, ceiling, floor, sofa, shelves, picture frames — across the seated 180° front field, with every path converging on the pile inside the 58° × 54° core of the glasses' 70° view. The game loop (rounds, waves with an in-wave speed ramp, combo timer, scoring with accuracy stats, round-end bonuses, game over and restart) was built and balanced first as a fast 2D prototype of the exact same rules, then fitted to the layered field of view and verified with a seated end-to-end test inside a taped 2-foot radius.
Devpost field · About the project

Challenges I ran into

The narrow field of view was the big one. The first design played everything in one wide cone; on the glasses that put feedback and even the pile at or beyond the visible edge — but shrinking the whole game into the middle would have thrown away the room-invasion spectacle. The fix was a layered design: the invasion fills a seated 180° front field (the competition's front-only rule, and nothing behind the player), the glasses show a 70° view of it, and everything essential — pile low-centre, gun, HUD, menus, and every beetle's final approach — lives inside a 58° × 54° core, proven with a seated test protocol. The potato economy was the second: early on it was too easy to shoot yourself into a loss, so ammo costs, the between-wave resupply and the round-end Restock bonus were tuned until firing felt free but never free of consequence. And as a first VR app, keeping every interaction hands-only — no controller or keyboard fallback anywhere, menus included — forced the interface down to a few big, honest pinch targets.
Devpost field · About the project

Accomplishments I'm proud of

A complete loop, start to game over to restart, that never asks for a controller. The potato economy working as a real decision rather than a gimmick — players hesitate before a sweet-potato shot, which is exactly the feeling the game was built around. And the comfort pass: a game fitted to the glasses' actual field of view and a chair, verified seated, instead of a standing game with a “sit down if you like” note.
Devpost field · About the project

What I learned

Design for the field of view first and the game second — on narrow-FOV glasses, where things are allowed to appear is the core design decision, not a polish step. A resource that is also your ammunition creates tension for free, with no extra systems. And hands-only design is a constraint that improves everything it touches: if a menu needs more than one big pinch target, the menu is wrong, not the hand.
Devpost field · About the project

What's next

More of the room in the game: beetles that use vertical surfaces and hide behind real furniture, a beetle that carries potatoes back visibly so you can intercept the theft, and seasonal piles (harvest events) beyond the competition build. First, though: wider seated playtesting to tune wave pacing and combo timing from real runs.

Day 4 · The full game loop

Start to game over — and straight back in

Everything a judge touches is hands-only, menus included: every choice is one big pinch target, at least a knuckle wide, with nothing hidden behind hover, keyboard, or a controller. The same flow runs in the prototype above.

1 · Rounds & waves

3 waves, then a breather

Each round is 3 waves. Beetles get faster and more numerous every wave — and speed also ramps inside a wave, so the last beetles of a wave are the quickest.

2 · Combos

Chain hits, raise the multiplier

Every 5 chained hits raises your score multiplier, up to ×5. Let the combo timer run out — or let a beetle steal — and it resets to ×1. Risk and reward in one glance.

3 · Scoring

Points with a paper trail

Crawler 10 · Dasher 15 · Tank 25 · Golden 50 (+3 🥔), all multiplied by your combo. Wave clear +25, round clear +100 — with shots, hits, and accuracy tracked live.

4 · Harvest Choice & restart

Pick an upgrade, or start over

Clear a round (v10) and the action freezes on the Harvest Choice: three big cards drawn from a pool of eight run-long upgrades — Stockpile, Bigger Splash, Golden Touch, Light Heavy… — with the next round's newcomers previewed above them. Pile hits zero? Game over — one pinch restarts.

The game in 30 seconds

One pile. Two ways to lose it.

That's the whole tension — and why this isn't just another wave shooter. Shooting and surviving draw from the same resource, so every pinch is a decision.

1

They emerge from your room

Beetles burst from real surfaces — walls, ceiling, floor, sofa, shelves, picture frames — using scene understanding, across the whole 180° front field of a seated player, then converge on the pile inside the 58° × 54° core.

2

Two hands work the gun

No controllers, no menus in the moment. Lead hand aims; support hand grabs a potato from the pile and drops it in — it loads itself — and a pinch on the trigger fires. Each grab deducts from the pile you're defending.

3

They grab and run

A beetle that reaches the pile hauls a potato back to its hole. Let too many through — or spray too wildly — and the pile is gone. Waves escalate in speed, numbers, and beetle types.

⭐ Why this can stand out in 650+ entries

Instantly readable: "Critters are stealing your potatoes — shoot them" lands in the first five minutes of judging, no tutorial essay needed.

A real mechanic, not a reskin: the ammo is the thing being stolen. Prior MR critter games proved judges like the loop; the potato economy is what's new.

Built for the glasses: seated design fitted to the 58° × 54° safe area and a 2 ft reach radius fits the narrow field of view instead of fighting it — nothing ever spawns behind you or at an edge.

Seated play space — 180° field out front, play in the core, 2 ft radius

The top-down cone is the shooting core; the invasion itself fills the 180° front field around it (never behind the chair), seen through the 70° glasses view. Everything reachable — pile, gun, both hands — sits inside a 2 ft radius around the chair. Comfortable seated, safe in a real living room, and legible on a narrow FOV.

Ammo types

Three potatoes, three decisions

Russet — the standard

Reliable single-target spud. The default pinch shot, and the baseline every other ammo is judged against.

  • Cost: 1 potato
  • Damage: 1 hit
  • Best for: crawlers, saving the pile

Sweet Potato — the splash

Bursts on impact and splats a cluster. Expensive — fire it into a crowd or not at all.

  • Cost: 2 potatoes
  • Damage: splash radius
  • Best for: packed waves, dashers

French Fry — the hose

Rapid-fire fries for panic moments. Light damage, high rate — easy to drain the pile if you hold it down.

  • Cost: 1 per burst
  • Damage: light, very fast
  • Best for: finishing, golden beetles

Try all three in the prototype above — the ammo buttons there use these same costs.

The opposition

Beetle bestiary

Crawler Wave 1+

The classic Colorado potato beetle. Slow, steady, comes in numbers. Teaches aiming and the cost of a miss.

Dasher Wave 3+

Zigzags toward the pile at double speed. Punishes slow aim; sweet-potato splash and fry bursts shine here.

Tank Beetle Wave 5+

Big, armoured, takes three russet hits. Slow enough that the real question is whether it's worth the potatoes.

Golden Beetle Rare · any wave

Fast, rare, and shiny. Splat it for bonus points and a small potato drop — the risk/reward moment judges remember.

Weaver Wave 1+ · new in v5

Leaf-green and broad, swaying side to side across the whole crawl in. Not fast — just never quite where your last shot expected it. Lead it, or splash it.

Hopper Wave 2+ · new in v5

Rust-orange, tall-shouldered, moves in crouch-and-spring bursts across the floor — sitting still, then suddenly two feet closer. Shoot it during the crouch, not the spring.

Pop Beetle Round 2+ · new in v10

The chain engine. It inflates and beeps faster as it closes on the pile. Shot dead it explodes and damages everything nearby — other Pops chain into it. Reach the pile alive and it detonates for −2 potatoes. The correct play flips with distance: far away it's a free bomb, close up it's a threat.

Brood Beetle Round 2+ · new in v10

A fat, slow splitter — killing it is only the start. On death it bursts into 4 larvae (tiny, fast, 5 pts each) that scatter straight for the pile. Kill it far out, or land a splash or HEAVY blast that clears the whole family at once. Where you kill it is the decision.

Husk Beetle Round 3+ · new in v10.14

A pale shell over a 1 HP body: two hits crack it in stages with no body damage — a HEAVY breaks it in one. The moment it cracks open it enrages: ~2.2× speed, straight at the pile, no weaving. Spend the shots early, or stop a charge at the door.

Spitter Beetle Round 4+ · new in v10.14

The ranged threat: it stops ~2.2 m from the pile and lobs a glowing blob every ~4 seconds — a landing splashes a potato away. The blob is a target too: shoot it mid-air for an INTERCEPTED bonus. It never steals and never comes closer. 2 HP.

Escalation

Waves get rude, gradually

Design targets: Dashers join at Wave 3, Tanks at Wave 5, speed creeps up each wave, and a resupply (+6 🥔) lands between waves — if your pile survives. The v10 builds add the composition rule on top: Brood Beetles join at total wave 5 and Pop Beetles at total wave 7 (both from Round 2 in AR), so later waves get ruder by mixing demands, not just by count.
